title: Sleep Staging Is Not Guesswork

reading.body:
A smart ring company's sleep-tracking system made a claim of 95 percent accuracy in identifying sleep stages, but a lawsuit alleges the artificial intelligence underlying this measurement amounts to guessing without access to the physiological signals that clinical sleep labs use. The company's devices measure heart rate, movement, and temperature, while hospital labs use electrodes to detect brain activity. Whether the company's proprietary method can actually achieve the claimed accuracy compared to clinical standards is not established.

The failure here sits in the claim itself. A deployed AI system made a specific accuracy assertion about a medical measurement without disclosing how far its input signals diverge from the diagnostic standard. This would have required either independent validation that the claimed accuracy held despite the signal gap, or restraint in what the company publicly stated about its device's capability. Whether peer-reviewed studies support the company's position, or whether those studies adequately addressed the signal limitation, is not established by the reporting.

reports.title: Oura, Smart Ring Maker, Sued for Alleged False Claims and Unreliable AI
Oura faces lawsuit accusing it of misleading consumers about sleep-tracking accuracy

summary:
A lawsuit filed by Clarkson Law Firm in San Francisco accuses Oura, a smart ring company valued at $11 billion, of false advertising regarding its sleep tracking capabilities. The suit alleges that Oura's rings, priced at $300 and up, cannot accurately measure different sleep stages as the company claims. Instead, the lawsuit contends that Oura's artificial intelligence relies on guesses comparable to coin flips, lacking the physiological signals that hospital sleep labs use to detect sleep stages. Oura markets its products as having 95 percent sleep staging accuracy compared to clinical sleep labs, but the lawsuit points out that actual sleep labs require multiple electrodes to measure brain activity, which Oura's devices lack.

Oura denied the allegations and stated that its sleep staging has been validated through peer-reviewed independent studies and compares favorably to polysomnography, the gold standard for sleep measurement. The company emphasized that its rings use multiple physiological signals including heart rate, movement, and temperature to estimate sleep stages. It remains unclear whether customers can join the class action suit or what compensation might be available if the case proceeds or settles. This lawsuit follows another ongoing class action against Oura for allegedly collecting personal information without consent for two years.
